cards.explanation: The answer is slaves. Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he says before they knew God, “…you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods.” That's a heavy word, and he picked it on purpose. Now you see why what comes next matters so much to him.

The answer is going back to weak and worthless principles. Paul asks, “…how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles?” Notice the words turning back. They know God now, and I think Paul is stunned they'd go back to those principles.

The answer is True. Paul asks, “Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?” It's a question, and I think he asks it so they'll stop and look at where they're headed. I bet hearing the word enslaved out loud lands hard.

The answer is fears. Paul says, “I fear for you…” and that comes right after he lists the days and months and seasons and years. That's a man who's worried because he cares, friends. A shrug would have been easier for him.

The answer is True. Paul says his fear is “…that my efforts for you may have been in vain.” He worked hard for these folks, and now he's worried it might not have stuck. I think anybody who's ever poured time into someone knows that ache.

The answer is False. Paul says, “You have done me no wrong.” That comes right after he begs them, “…become like me, for I became like you.” So the Galatians haven't wronged him, and that's straight from Paul.

The answer is because of an illness. Paul says, “You know that it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you.” He doesn't hide it, and he doesn't make it fancy. Sometimes the story starts with a rough moment, and that's okay.

The answer is as if he were an angel of God. Paul says they “…welcomed me as if I were an angel of God…” and he adds, “…as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” Paul says it was because of an illness that he first preached the gospel to them, and that's how they welcomed him. I think that tells you how warm it was.

The answer is True. Paul says they welcomed him “…as if I were Christ Jesus Himself.” He says it was because of an illness that he first preached the gospel to them, and they welcomed him like that. It's the kind of welcome I'd have fallen over for after all my years stuck in the back of a junk drawer.

The answer is their own eyes. Paul says, “…if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.” Notice the “…if it were possible…” He's saying how deep their care ran, so I think he wants them to remember it.

The answer is enemy. Paul asks, “Have I now become your enemy by telling you the truth?” It's a question, and I think it stings, since they once welcomed him “…as if I were an angel of God…” That's quite a change to ask about.

The answer is isolate them from us. Paul says, “…they want to isolate you from us, so that you may be zealous for them.” They want the Galatians cut off from “us,” and the goal is that the Galatians be zealous for them. It's like someone moving you to a quiet table so only they can talk to you.

The answer is True. Paul says they want to isolate the Galatians “…so that you may be zealous for them.” Their goal, in Paul's words, is that the Galatians be zealous for them. I think Paul sees it clearly, and he wants the Galatians to see it too.
The answer is False. Paul says, “…it is good to be zealous if it serves a noble purpose…” So zeal can be a fine thing. The question he's raising is what it serves.

The answer is at any time and not just when he's with them. Paul says it's good to be zealous for a noble purpose, “…at any time, and not only when I am with you.” In other words, that zeal isn't meant to depend on him being there. It's the same zeal whether Paul is around or not.

The answer is childbirth. Paul writes, “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you…” That's a picture of deep, hard-working love. Nobody says it about people they don't care about.

The answer is True. Paul says he's in those pains “…until Christ is formed in you…” He doesn't give a finish line other than that. He keeps caring until Christ is formed in them, and I think that says a lot about his heart.

The answer is his tone. Paul says, “…how I wish I could be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you.” I think a letter is hard because you can't see a face while you say a hard thing. Being there with them is how he wishes he could change it.
